item.title: Thriving koala population near major NSW city could be chlamydia-free
item.description: Chlamydia poses a deadly threat to koalas, but researchers believe they have found a disease-free population near Newcastle. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Laurise Dickson

item.title: NASA Announces X-70 Experimental Aircraft to Advance Flight Research
item.description: On Wednesday, NASA unveiled its newest experimental aircraft, the X-70 Fractal, during the UP.Summit at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. This high-performance, highly adaptable research platform is designed to accelerate the development and testing of advanced aviation technologies. The crewed X-70 features advanced, rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology that will allow NASA to explore […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Cheryl Warner

item.title: Japan's ALS community is ready to become research partners, nationwide survey suggests
item.description: People living with ALS and their families in Japan are eager to help shape research on the disease, even though most have never heard of patient and public involvement (PPI), according to a study published on Oct. 30, 2026, in Research Involvement and Engagement. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new route to calculating gluon production in proton–nucleus collisions
item.description: In the theoretical study of proton-nucleus collisions, the colliding projectiles can be described as streams of color charges moving along their respective trajectories. These color charges couple to gluons, which then produce the particles that are observed in the final state (gluons and quarks, which eventually produce hadrons). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earth atmosphere emulators could enable faster and more accurate weather predictions
item.description: If you partitioned the entire Earth, from just below the surface to the top of the atmosphere, into 1-kilometer-square chunks, there would be billions of them. Now run each of those cells through a series of complex physics equations, and you can see how the entire Earth system interacts and evolves in detail, one step at a time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: European orbiter detects fresh hints of volcanic activity on Mars
item.description: New evidence from gas seeping above volcanic rifts suggests Mars is not geologically dead deep inside, but merely sleeping. Fresh fissures along the Alba Mons region hint at active spots under the surface, where gases from inside the planet may be making their way up to the surface. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How ranchers on Brazil's 'Dirty List' bypass forced labor safeguards by selling cattle through intermediaries
item.description: Brazil's "Dirty List," a public registry that names employers found to have violated anti-slavery laws, is a key component of the country's efforts to combat forced labor. Major meatpackers in Brazil signed sustainable sourcing commitments promising to not purchase cattle directly from ranchers on the Dirty List. But new research shows that ranchers have found ways around these restrictions, rerouting cattle through intermediaries and allowing cattle linked to forced labor to remain in domestic and international beef and leather supply chains. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: First direct observations reveal hydrogen dissolved in tiny gaps between metal atoms
item.description: University of Sydney researchers have made a breakthrough by directly observing hydrogen in the tiny spaces between the atoms in metal alloys. The world-first observation of hydrogen dissolving in these 'metal crystal lattices' offers fresh insights into why hydrogen can weaken metals and how more hydrogen-resistant materials might be developed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists reveal how cosignaling receptors dually regulate T cell activation via phase separation
item.description: Previous studies have shown that upon antigen stimulation, the T cell receptor (TCR) undergoes phase separation with the kinase Lck to mediate rapid T cell activation. However, the manner in which costimulating receptors regulate this process has remained unclear. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient coins suggest influential Iron Age king was female
item.description: Bournemouth University (BU) archaeological research has revealed that Iron Age British ruler "Verica," who was central to the Roman invasion of Britain in A.D. 43, was in fact a woman. This discovery rewrites the history of early Roman Britain. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When customers cross the line: Study reveals hidden toll of harassment on gig workers
item.description: A rideshare driver picks up a passenger who makes repeated unwanted sexual comments. The ride ends, but the experience doesn't. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Using ChatGPT at work? Your boss may trust you less, new study finds
item.description: Artificial intelligence may be making employees faster and more productive, but it could also be quietly damaging their careers. A new study led by Samuel Meyers, a Ph.D. student, together with his adviser Dr. Yochanan Bigman of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and Dr. Roman Briker of WHU—Otto Beisheim School of Management in Germany, suggests that workers who use ChatGPT and other AI tools may pay an unexpected professional price: their managers are less likely to trust them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nasa’s 22-year-old Swift satellite telescope falls from orbit in fiery finale
item.description: Nasa’s Swift satellite ⁠telescope, which spent two decades studying the most powerful known blasts of energy in the cosmos, tumbled out of orbit as expected on Wednesday and burned up in Earth’s atmosphere over Indonesia, the space agency reported. The fiery demise of the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, weighing roughly 3,200 pounds (1,452kg), came less than three months after a ‌rescue spacecraft failed its mission to boost the satellite to higher orbit and extend its life. The US Space Force... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Entrepreneurs who struggle to understand their emotions are less committed to their business goals, study finds
item.description: Entrepreneurs who struggle to recognize and make sense of their own emotions are less likely to feel attached to their businesses and less committed to achieving their goals, particularly in high-stress periods, according to new research from the University of Bath School of Management. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Genetic interaction map could lead to better antibiotic pairings for tuberculosis
item.description: Rockefeller scientists have created the most comprehensive map to date of how essential genes interact in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the bacterium responsible for tuberculosis (TB). The unprecedented map reveals thousands of previously unknown genetic relationships, offering a new window into the inner workings of one of the world's deadliest pathogens. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Swift telescope plummets to Earth over Indonesia
item.description: NASA's Swift telescope has re-entered Earth's atmosphere near Sumatra in Indonesia following a failed rescue attempt earlier this year. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.title: A carefully timed pair of light pulses can amplify the motion of atomic layers in a quantum material
item.description: The principle "Work smarter, not harder!" apparently also applies to controlling quantum materials with light. Many of their fascinating properties depend on how the atoms are arranged in the crystal. Ultrashort laser pulses can be used to alter these structures in a targeted way—the light first excites electrons, whose changed energy and dynamics exert forces on the atomic nuclei and can thereby set the atoms in motion. Such processes unfold within femtoseconds, a millionth of a billionth of a second. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA navigation experiment shows promise for planetary landings
item.description: NASA has successfully demonstrated technology designed to help spacecraft autonomously navigate to safe landing sites on the moon and on other planets. An Alta-X drone equipped with the agency's Safe and Precise Landing—Integrated Capabilities Evolution (SPLICE) guidance, navigation and control payload completed simulated lunar descent and landing maneuvers Aug. 27. The flight took place at Rogers Dry Lake near NASA's Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Flat feet may have helped Neanderthals stay stable while carrying heavy loads
item.description: In all likelihood, the Neanderthals had flat feet. But it was not a defect at all. Instead, it was the consequence of a precise functional strategy to reduce impact stress under heavy loads and maximize stability on mountainous or rough terrain. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hundreds of Ice Age rock art engravings discovered hidden in plain sight
item.description: Archaeologists have discovered the third-largest assemblage of Ice Age cave art ever found in Mediterranean Iberia in a region thought devoid of cave art, transforming our knowledge of Paleolithic European art. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Trust in influencers grows more important in predicting buying intentions over time, analysis finds
item.description: A meta-analysis of empirical studies involving more than 31,000 participants has revealed the factors that affect the level of influence of so-called social media influencers. Those factors include credibility, expertise, attractiveness and perceived similarity to their followers. They are, the work shows, positively associated with the attitude of consumers toward the brands mentioned or promoted by those influencers and, in turn, their purchasing intentions. Details of the analysis are published in the International Journal of Internet Marketing and Advertising. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Carbon dots fluoresce their way through the rainbow as liquids change
item.description: Fluorescent materials usually emit a single consistent color. They are typically made from dyes or metallic components. In contrast, researchers reporting in ACS Central Science have created carbon dots that can fluoresce in a range of colors under UV light, depending on the concentration and the liquid they're in. The team incorporated the new carbon dots into plastic decorations and used them to create a data encryption system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new superinductor created within a silicon integrated circuit
item.description: A recent study published in Nature Electronics and carried out by researchers from nanoGUNE's Quantum Hardware research group, Quantum Motion, London Center for Nanotechnology, Imperial College London and the University of Cambridge introduces a new superinductor created within a silicon integrated circuit fabricated in a commercial complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) process. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Feejee Mermaid on display in Colorado may shock and intrigue—but no longer considered a 'missing link'
item.description: Mermaids have inhabited world folklore and mythology for centuries. Ancient Babylonians worshiped Oannes, a human-fish hybrid; sirens populated Greek mythology; and fairy tales such as "The Little Mermaid" have made this figure a pop culture icon. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cosmic hydrogen measurement marks breakthrough in mapping the universe
item.description: An international research project is bringing scientists closer to mapping the universe. The MeerKLASS Collaboration has reported its first measurement of the large-scale clustering of cosmic hydrogen, advancing a technique that could transform how cosmologists chart the universe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Corporate green reports: Do independent checks really help companies deliver measurable action?
item.description: The European Union's Omnibus reform has exempted most of the companies it once covered from mandatory sustainability reporting under the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD). It has also dropped plans for tougher "reasonable" assurance checks on green claims, which come closer to a full audit. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Traditional Korean paper becomes breathable patch for future wearable health care
item.description: Wearable health-monitoring devices are becoming increasingly important for personalized health care, but conventional patches often rely on substrates that restrict airflow, trap sweat and cause skin discomfort during prolonged use. These limitations can also interfere with the reliable collection and analysis of sweat, highlighting the need for breathable materials that support both comfortable wear and accurate sensing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NOAA, NASA release measurements of 2026 ozone hole
item.description: Atypical weather conditions caused the Antarctic ozone hole to grow to an unusually large size in 2026, NOAA and NASA scientists reported today, though they said the protective ozone layer is still on track to recover by later this century. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Molecular choreography: How the p97 protein regulates cellular quality control
item.description: The p97 protein plays a central role in cellular quality control by preparing defective or no-longer-needed proteins for degradation and recycling. Researchers at the University of Münster, in collaboration with the University of Duisburg-Essen, have investigated how p97 and its auxiliary proteins interact in this process. The study has now been published in the journal Nature Communications. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: El Pago Carnes a la Leña abrirá este 7 y 8 de noviembre su sucursal en el municipio de Yotala, con gastronomía, cultura y las tradiciones chaqueñas, de la mano del Centro Cultural…

item.title: How a moth 'maelstrom' gave scientists hope for an endangered species
item.description: A swarm of thousands filmed on a Victorian mountain top is part of a surge in bogong moth sightings, which researchers say is good news for the endangered mountain pygmy possum. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Philippe Perez

item.title: Bio-based smart coating combines fire protection, early warning and upcyclability
item.description: Researchers have developed a multifunctional fire-protective coating that not only shields materials from extreme heat but also provides an early warning of fire and can be recycled into new flame-retardant materials at the end of its life. The work, published in Polymer Degradation and Stability, demonstrates a strategy for combining fire safety, sustainability and circularity within a single material system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New research uncovers chiral topological phases in metals without structural order
item.description: Fermions are among the most important particles in physics and include both everyday electrons and more exotic variants. Chiral fermions, like gloves, come in left- and right-handed versions and were proposed over a century ago. While high-energy neutrinos—the leading candidates for massless chiral fermions—proved to have mass, nearly (semi-) metallic solid-state crystals were discovered 15 years ago to host electronic versions of massless chiral fermions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Shares Plans to Accelerate Artemis, Return to Moon
item.description: In an update on Oct. 23, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and other agency leaders shared the agency’s path to returning Americans to the lunar surface in 2028. Agency leadership provided updates on the previously announced acceleration plans for the Artemis program, advancing toward the agency’s Artemis III test flight in 2027 and Artemis IV Moon […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Lee Mohon

item.title: Why a company donating $20,000 a month counts for more than $240,000 once a year in the eyes of customers
item.description: People tend to think more highly of companies that give to charity on a monthly or weekly basis rather than donating an annual lump sum worth the same amount. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A cosmic 'leaf blower': Light-propelled winds help explain early universe's bright galaxies
item.description: When astronomers looked at photos of the early universe taken by the James Webb Space Telescope, they found something odd: an overabundance of bright galaxies. Based on what they knew about the early universe, such galaxies should have been far less common in the few hundred million years following the Big Bang. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA space telescope plunges to Earth after two decades studying cosmic explosions
item.description: One of NASA's premier space telescopes plunged to Earth on Wednesday, ending its 22-year investigation of the universe's biggest explosions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New data infrastructure service strengthens interdisciplinary research
item.description: The "Geolinking Service SoRa" research data infrastructure helps to close a gap in the German research landscape. Many questions—such as those regarding social inequality or environmental justice—can only be answered through interdisciplinary analyses, such as linking social science and spatial science data: Does the proportion of green space in a residential neighborhood affect health and well-being? Are people who live in single-family homes happier than residents of densely built-up urban neighborhoods? How does transportation infrastructure—such as access to buses and trains—influence… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Evolution has repeatedly turned hawkmoth genitals into defensive tools
item.description: The genital structures of male hawkmoths are lifesavers. By rubbing specialized scales on their genitals against parts of their abdomen, the nocturnal insects emit ultrasonic sounds that can potentially scramble the acoustic signals that bats use to hunt. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Northern permafrost greening masks declining plant resilience, study finds
item.description: An international study jointly led by researchers from the Department of Geography and the Institute for Climate and Carbon Neutrality at the Faculty of Social Sciences, The University of Hong Kong (HKU), has revealed that vegetation resilience across Northern Hemisphere permafrost regions underwent a widespread reversal around 2008, declining broadly despite continued greening. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Gold mining introduces an overlooked threat to wild caimans
item.description: Mercury pollution from artisanal gold mining in tropical regions is finding its way into wildlife. A team from the University of Vienna and the Veterinary University of Vienna shows that mercury exposure impairs the glucocorticoid response that helps animals cope with acute stress. This weakened stress response could reduce the caimans' chances of survival and reproduction. The findings, recently published in the journal Communications Biology, point to a previously overlooked endocrine threat to crocodylians. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Overlooked insects are bucking the trend and becoming more abundant, study finds
item.description: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that many of Britain's overlooked insects and spiders are becoming more abundant and emerging earlier in the year, according to a new study. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New CO₂ sensor combines high sensitivity with a wider measurement range
item.description: Researchers from the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science (HFIPS) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) have developed a carbon dioxide (CO₂) sensor that combines high sensitivity with a wider measurement range. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Massop Legacy Park Dedication: Iowa family gift turns land into public nature area; future trails eyed
item.description: A family in Iowa has donated 3.53 acres of land to Buena Vista County to create Massop Legacy Park. This new public space aims to provide future generations with access to nature and preserve local wildlife habitats. Conservation efforts will focus on enhancing native vegetation and improving water quality along Owl Lake Creek. The park is envisioned to eventually connect with a larger recreational network around Storm Lake. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Unveiling the science behind a beautiful singing voice
item.description: Expert listeners can often form an immediate impression of a singer's performance. But what exactly in the voice drives that judgment? In classical vocal competitions, performers are rated on an overall score. However, the criteria behind that score are rarely made explicit. Moreover, voice quality is often described in vague, metaphorical terms, such as "ringing," "warm" or "focused," which can mean different things to different listeners. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AlphaFold 3 predicts complex immune interactions using protein sequences alone
item.description: Researchers at the Translational Genomics Research Institute (TGen), part of City of Hope, have developed a new approach using the artificial intelligence platform AlphaFold 3 to predict whether a T cell receptor will recognize a specific antigen based solely on its genetic sequence. The advancement could help scientists more rapidly decode immune responses to infectious diseases, tumors and other health threats. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Race, age and gender associated with experiences of harassment among gig workers
item.description: The gig economy is rapidly growing, and scholars are still working to understand the conditions gig workers encounter. Julieta Aguilar at the University of Kentucky, U.S., and Dr. Jeremy Reynolds at Purdue University, U.S., examined experiences of harassment in the gig economy. Their study, published on Nov. 4, 2026, in the journal PLOS One, found associations between race, gender, age and reported experiences of harassment, indicating that already precarious employment may be even more fraught for some workers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Some cats are shy, just like human infants
item.description: Some cats display a complex mixture of fear and curiosity, which is similar to shyness observed in human infants, according to a study published Nov. 4, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Madoka Hattori at Kyoto University, Japan, and colleagues. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Big extended families help adult female ground squirrels survive hibernation
item.description: For Belding's ground squirrels, adult females are more likely to survive from year to year if they live near more adult female kin—but neither males nor young females get the same boost from nearby family. Jill Mateo and colleagues at the University of Chicago, U.S., report these findings on Nov. 4, 2026, in the journal PLOS One. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A 7,000-year-old piece of leather reveals a deep history of Spanish goats
item.description: Ancient DNA reveals that denizens of the Iberian Peninsula made leather from domestic goats as far back as 7,000 years ago, according to a study published Nov. 4, 2026, in the journal PLOS One by Jolijn A. M. Erven of University College Dublin, Ireland, and colleagues. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover there are way more bugs in California than you thought
item.description: A new study published in the journal Ecography finds that there are more than 60,000 different species of insects in California—and scientists have only described about two-thirds of them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Five things to know about guiding sound for better communication
item.description: Every time someone picks up a call, the phone does a quiet bit of translation. Incoming radio signals are converted into tiny sound waves that ripple across chips before being turned back into data. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Molecular imaging reveals how shape-shifting protein complex captures DNA and holds separate sections together
item.description: Researchers at Kanazawa University and the National Institute of Genetics in Japan have used high-speed atomic force microscopy to observe how a group of proteins known as Smc5/6 interacts with DNA. The images reveal how this structure opens and closes, captures DNA and brings separate sections together. The researchers also observed Smc5/6 holding twisted sections of DNA in place, producing more tightly packed arrangements. The findings, published in Nature Communications, provide new insights into the molecular processes that contribute to the maintenance and repair of genetic material. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How a cell surface protein slows down the Ebola virus
item.description: The Ebola virus can cause severe, often life-threatening disease in humans. To replicate, it must enter human cells and exploit their cellular processes. In doing so, it encounters natural defense mechanisms that can make infection more difficult. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: This fruit fly's aphrodisiac reveals how social and environmental context shape mating practices
item.description: Imagine a crowded dance floor where bodies move to the beat beneath a glittering disco ball. Some of the dancers pair up, drawn together by the heady atmosphere. For flies, as for humans, the right atmosphere can serve as a potent aphrodisiac. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Announces Ka-Band Satellite Relay Awards for Space Communications
item.description: NASA selected three companies on Wednesday to perform work to develop Ka-band space relay capability concepts that are compatible with current missions in space, ensuring service continuity for existing spacecraft without requiring modifications to their onboard systems. Through this work, NASA will aim to acquire end-to-end solutions that include space, ground, launch, operations, and integration […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Taveau

item.title: Overlooked Melbourne patch reveals 45 animal species and more than 40 plant types
item.description: When we think about nature in our cities, what often comes to mind are parks and reserves—planned, managed and clearly marked spaces that support animal and plant life in our urban environment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Satellite analysis finds little evidence that data centers cause widespread ground warming
item.description: A new study published in Environmental Research Letters has found little evidence that hyperscale data centers cause significant heating of surrounding land. While a previous study suggested data centers heat surrounding land by about 2 °C on average (up to 9 °C), reaching 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) away, 13 years of satellite data reveal that server waste heat causes minimal nighttime surface warming, while building materials actually cool ground temperatures during the day. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fireworks provide a few minutes of joy, but the economic and environmental costs last much longer
item.description: Every Bonfire Night, people pay for a box of fireworks so their friends and family can enjoy the colorful display. Within a few minutes, it's all over. But the price on the box doesn't reflect the hidden costs: the smoke inhaled by neighbors, the animals disturbed or the public services called out when things go wrong. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Space Grant Students Fuel Agency’s Inspiration Tour
item.description: NASA’s Inspiration Tour spread the excitement of space exploration and aeronautical innovation by connecting the public, industry, and academia with the people, technologies, and organizations that drive American leadership in space. At nearly every stop across the country, NASA Space Grant has brought students into the heart of the action. In Iowa, NASA Administrator Jared […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Sandra May

item.title: Hubble Reveals Cosmic Mystery
item.description: This photo released on Nov. 2, 2026, showcases NGC 4449, a dwarf irregular. Researchers using NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies — small galaxies containing a few thousand to hundreds of millions of stars — including NGC 4449 and found that much of the oxygen they expected to see is missing. Read […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: We often think of extreme heat as simply uncomfortable, but for pregnant women the risks can be far more serious. Research has linked heat exposure to premature births. Access to…
item.description: We often think of extreme heat as simply uncomfortable, but for pregnant women the risks can be far more serious. Research has linked heat exposure to premature births. Access to shade, clean water and somewhere cool should never be a luxury. Black Lion Studios Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Secrets of the avian calendar: When do migratory birds have the opportunity to reset their schedule?
item.description: A team led by Vojtěch Brlík from Charles University in Czechia and the University of Guelph in Canada analyzed data from more than 2,300 birds tracked using miniature devices to find out how closely linked individual stages of the migratory birds' annual cycle are. The scientists were also interested in whether these linkages break down at a certain stage and whether late-departing individuals can make up for their delay. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new spin on catalysts: A roadmap for smarter chemical reactions
item.description: Electron spin is a quantum property that makes electrons behave like tiny magnets. It can influence how electrons interact with each other and how chemical reactions take place. But what does this have to do with producing fertilizers, making cleaner fuels or improving energy technologies? What connects all these processes is the use of catalysts, materials that help chemical reactions happen faster and more efficiently. By controlling electron spin, scientists may be able to improve how these catalysts work, opening up new possibilities for more efficient chemical processes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The DEA banned a drug some opioid users called a miracle
item.description: Researchers say the Schedule I ban could kill studies of a promising opioid treatment. Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Manisha Krishnan, wired.com

item.title: Lecturers and students see AI use very differently, study finds
item.description: Instructors and students have significantly different perceptions of how much generative artificial intelligence (AI) is being used in university studies, according to new research from The University of Manchester and Spain's Universidad del Pais Vasco/Euskal Herriko Unibertsitatea. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wild animals can now GPS-collar themselves for research
item.description: For six decades, wildlife researchers have faced a persistent challenge: to attach a tracking device to study a wild animal, they first have to catch it. Now, a new approach developed at the Norwegian University of Life Sciences (NMBU) allows GPS collars to be deployed autonomously on free-roaming terrestrial wildlife. Published in BioScience, the proof-of-concept study demonstrates Capture-Free Telemetry (CFT), a technique that places tracking devices on wild animals as they interact with baited deployment units in their natural habitat. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Millions of bogong moths are blanketing cities in Australia, and they are still endangered
item.description: In recent weeks, people across Australia have found fluttering bogong moths (Agrotis infusa) in their homes, cars and even bedrooms. These insects have embarked on their annual migration from breeding grounds across southern Australia to the cool caves of the Australian Alps. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Seagrass helps Biscayne Bay's mangroves keep up with rising seas
item.description: The mangroves of Biscayne Bay have been getting help from an unlikely neighbor—the seagrass meadows just offshore. Dead seagrass blades and seaweed drift loose until the tide carries them into the mangroves, where they pile up, rot slowly and then become part of the ground. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study reveals how five tuna species respond to changing Mediterranean conditions
item.description: As the Mediterranean Sea continues to warm, it may become more favorable for some tropical tuna species. However, warmer waters do not necessarily provide all the environmental conditions these highly migratory fish need. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: CT scans reveal four-letter code to 400-year-old lock from Welsh shipwreck
item.description: Experts from Amgueddfa Cymru and Cardiff University have used cutting-edge CT scanning technology to unlock a centuries-old combination lock recovered from one of Wales' most remarkable maritime discoveries. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Smiling can make you happier—unless someone forces you to do it
item.description: Nicholas Coles, Ph.D., had long heard that forcing a smile can make you feel a little happier—after all, he had done a lot of the research that supposedly proved it. But something didn't sit quite right with his own findings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists develop novel model to forecast internal solitary waves from multiple sources in the Sulu Sea
item.description: A research team led by Professor Li Xiaofeng from the Institute of Oceanology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (IOCAS) has developed a model to forecast internal solitary waves originating from multiple sources in the Sulu Sea. The model combines physical equations and satellite observations to predict wave arrival times and crest positions across this complex marine environment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Does opting out of TV tracking work?
item.description: The fact our TVs are gathering our information isn't new, but what and how they're tracking - and if we can stop it - is hard to figure out. Researchers at Northeastern University monitored 12 TVs from 10 manufacturers to test whether opting out of automatic content recognition (ACR) actually works. While opting out was […] Fuente: The Verge.
item.dc:creator: John Higgins

item.title: Tiny melt traces shed light on the Colorado Plateau's explosive past
item.description: Deep beneath Earth's surface, some minerals hold clues to processes that happened millions of years ago. One such mineral is lawsonite, which forms under high pressure and relatively low temperatures. What makes it significant is its ability to store water within its crystal structure and carry it deep into Earth as tectonic plates move beneath one another. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Limited cold stress during pregnancy could lead to increased lamb birth weight, survivability
item.description: Research out of South Dakota State University has highlighted a potential connection between limited exposure to cold stress during pregnancy and birth weight. The work showed that shearing ewes at day 50 of gestation, rather than after 100 days, resulted in larger and heavier lambs at birth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A surprising discovery could help aging muscles repair themselves
item.description: Scientists have discovered a compound that transforms a natural muscle-repair protein into a more powerful version dubbed "Super HGF," more than doubling its ability to bind to a key receptor while protecting it from age-related chemical damage. The breakthrough, supported by early mouse experiments, could eventually help combat muscle loss and preserve strength as people age. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired
item.description: Scientists propose that the brain’s mysterious cross-wiring, which connects each hemisphere to the opposite side of the body, may have originated more than 500 million years ago in the visual systems of ancient fish. Rather than evolving for a specific advantage, this unusual arrangement may simply be a legacy of evolution building new brain circuits on an ancient foundation. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Why AI influencers work better with a human friend
item.description: Scroll through Instagram long enough and you'll meet an influencer who isn't real. AI influencers—computer-generated personalities like Lil Miquela, who has millions of followers and has posted for Prada, Samsung and Dior—look and act like human creators, but they're entirely synthetic. Brands like them because they never go off-script, never age and never cause a scandal. Yet they share one stubborn weakness: people tend not to trust them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Permanent daylight saving time has a dark side, scientists warn
item.description: A new study warns that permanent daylight saving time could force American children to make at least 2 billion additional school commutes in darkness, potentially increasing safety risks and disrupting their biological clocks. Researchers found that fatal crashes involving school-aged pedestrians were roughly twice as likely during dark mornings as after sunrise. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: How to say 'no' to your child—and stick to it
item.description: "No" may be one of the hardest words for parents to say to a young child. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A tiny squeeze dramatically changes the magnetism of exotic materials
item.description: Scientists have discovered that a simple mechanical squeeze can dramatically alter the magnetic properties and electrical behavior of exotic materials called altermagnets. The surprising breakthrough could open the door to faster, more energy-efficient electronics and new technologies for quantum computing. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: MIT scientists break a 20-year rule and unlock never-before-seen crystal structures
item.description: MIT scientists have challenged two decades of conventional thinking by discovering that flexible molecular connections, rather than rigid ones, can unlock entirely new ways to arrange nanoparticles. The breakthrough could lead to a new generation of designer materials with unusual properties and applications in electronics, medicine, and energy. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Research reveals accelerating sea-level rise around Ireland
item.description: A new study led by the ICARUS Climate Research Center at Maynooth University in Ireland has reconstructed a century of Irish sea-level change, revealing a stark acceleration in sea-level rise. The research, titled "A Century of Sea-Level Change in Ireland (1925–2024)" and published in Ocean Science, combines tide-gauge records from six locations, including newly digitized historical records from Cork, Tarbert and Galway. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: "Todavía hoy me arrepiento": Spielberg aún se lamenta del impacto causado por esta obra maestra que puedes recuperar en streaming
item.description: En 2022, en el programa ‘Desert Island Discs’ de BBC Radio 4: Spielberg confesaba que todavía hoy lamenta la matanza de escualos que siguió a la publicación del libro de Peter Benchley y de su popularísima adaptación ' Tiburón ' (que puedes recatar en Movistar Plus y SkyShowtime ). "Lo lamento de verdad, sinceramente", dijo. Habló además de un temor peculiar: que los tiburones sigan enfadados con él por la fiebre de pesca deportiva que se desató a partir de 1975. Un estudio publicado en Nature en 2021 le quita buena parte del peso de encima: la abundancia de tiburones y rayas oceánicos ha… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: John Tones

item.title: Enjoyment increases consumers' willingness to pay for sustainable products
item.description: Consumers are more willing to pay for sustainable products if they also perceive them as enjoyable and appealing, according to a study conducted at the University of Eastern Finland. However, environmental friendliness alone does not always translate into willingness to pay. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Call adjustments help bats keep their echolocation signals distinct, study finds
item.description: Bats can produce ultrasonic pulses with high frequencies between 20,000 and 120,000 hertz, which are inaudible to humans. The sound waves they produce travel forward, hitting nearby objects and bouncing back in the form of echoes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Extreme heat is becoming a fact of life in more parts of the world, with serious implications for pregnant women and their babies.... Ver más
item.description: Extreme heat is becoming a fact of life in more parts of the world, with serious implications for pregnant women and their babies.... Ver más We often think of extreme heat as simply uncomfortable, but for pregnant women the risks can be far more serious. Research has linked heat exposure to premature births. Access to shade, clean water and somewhere cool should never be a luxury. Tenemos… Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: NASA is racing against time to save the Hubble Space Telescope
item.description: NASA is exploring a daring plan to save the legendary Hubble Space Telescope from its eventual fiery plunge into Earth's atmosphere. After more than 35 years of groundbreaking discoveries, Hubble is slowly losing altitude, and without intervention, it could fall back to Earth as early as 2033 or 2034. To keep the iconic observatory operating, NASA is asking private space companies to propose innovative ways to boost Hubble into a higher orbit, upgrade its capabilities, or safely dispose of it when its mission finally ends. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: SLAC scientists find conclusive proof of a mysterious third type of magnetism
item.description: For nearly 90 years, scientists believed magnetism fell into just two categories, but researchers have now confirmed a remarkable third type called altermagnetism. Using specialized X-rays, they uncovered a unique magnetic signature that proves these materials behave differently from conventional magnets. Altermagnets combine stability with the ability to efficiently carry information, potentially overcoming major limitations in today's electronics. The discovery could lead to faster computers, more efficient data centers, and breakthroughs in quantum technology. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Por increíble que parezca, hay gente comprando cadáveres de hace siglos en Facebook
item.description: En Facebook e Instagram se anuncian cabezas, manos y otros restos de cuerpos humanos a precios competitivos. Son piezas momificadas de hace siglos que se ofertan como si fueran objetos de segunda mano. Sin embargo, lo que parece una extravagancia macabra esconde un negocio internacional que los investigadores llevan años siguiendo. Y han encontrado algo más inquietante que cualquier maldición egipcia: unos hongos potencialmente peligrosos, sustancias tóxicas y restos humanos que viajan por correo hasta las casas de sus compradores. Momias a golpe de clic. Un estudio titulado The Real Mummy’s… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Miguel Jorge

item.title: Toxic air pollution surges in Indian capital
item.description: Toxic air pollution in India's capital, New Delhi, surged on Wednesday to more than 30 times the World Health Organization's recommended daily limit, data from air monitors showed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study calls for a rethink on how we manage the threats posed by hazardous species
item.description: While human well-being depends on the health of our ecosystems, there are also countless aspects of the natural world that pose serious threats to people. Every year, over 700,000 people die from diseases transmitted by animals, snakebites kill up to 500,000 people, and crop loss from pests carries an estimated cost of around $220 billion. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Six measures could save 1.6 million lives a year: WHO
item.description: Implementing a few climate and health measures could save nearly 1.6 million lives a year and generate trillions of dollars for the economy, the World Health Organization said Wednesday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Time to wake up MetOp-SG-B1 weather satellite
item.description: Following a short period in storage after arriving at Europe’s Spaceport in French Guiana, the MetOp Second Generation-B1 satellite has been transferred to a cleanroom and removed from its transport container. The team is now preparing to reactivate this ‘sleeping beauty, and begin the final checks and preparations ahead of its launch, planned towards the end of the year. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: AI helps Stanford scientists discover a “natural Ozempic” with a surprising advantage
item.description: Stanford researchers have discovered an AI-identified natural molecule that dramatically suppresses appetite and promotes fat loss in animals, potentially offering an Ozempic-like weight-loss treatment without common digestive side effects or significant muscle loss. Called BRP, the molecule reduced food intake by up to 50% and targets a different brain pathway, raising hopes for a more precise obesity treatment if future human trials prove successful. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: La Antártida esconde un secreto bajo sus suelos helados: el 91 % de las cepas de una bacteria analizada solo aparece allí
item.description: La Antártida se ve como un paraje donde solo se pueden encontrar pingüinos, pero la realidad es que también es una tierra que puede llegar a fascinar a cualquier microbiólogo por la adaptación que han sufrido diferentes bacterias. Tal es así que un nuevo análisis genético a gran escala hecho sobre los suelos de la Antártida ha demostrado que el continente helado tiene sus propias reglas, puesto que la inmensa mayoría de las cepas de un género bacteriano muy común en todo el mundo resulta ser endémico de estas tierras. El estudio. Ha sido publicado recientemente en la revista PNAS, y aporta… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: José A. Lizana

item.title: APOD: 2026 November 4 – The Not-So-Hidden Galaxy, IC 342
item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 4 – The… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. The Not-So-Hidden […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Before the Dawn in America’s Heartland
item.description: With hardly a cloud in sight, astronauts had a sweeping view of nighttime lights in the U.S. Midwest. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Testing Einstein's laws from the bottom of the Mediterranean Sea
item.description: Are the laws of physics truly the same everywhere in the universe? This fundamental principle, known as Lorentz invariance, lies at the heart of Einstein's theory of relativity. Yet some theories that seek to reconcile gravity with quantum physics suggest that it might not always hold. To investigate this possibility, researchers from the international KM3NeT collaboration analyzed 5,828 atmospheric neutrino candidate events detected by KM3NeT/ORCA, a neutrino telescope located deep in the Mediterranean Sea. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Loophole listing keeps seafood qualifying as critically endangered on the menu
item.description: One of Australia's most dangerously overfished species, redfish (Centroberyx affinis), will continue to be served on our dinner tables following its latest listing as "conservation dependent." The classification is a loophole allowing species that qualify for critically endangered listings and protections to instead be killed and sold for seafood. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A vampire burial: A Polish woman was buried with a sickle to stop her rising from the grave
item.description: Unveiled by time, Zosia's grave in Pień offers a glimpse into 17th century Polish traditions regarding death and the supernatural. Archaeologists found an iron sickle and a toe-bound padlock alongside her remains, suggesting efforts to prevent her from rising as a vampire. This peculiar burial practice hints at Zosia's affluent background, compelling researchers to dive deeper into her life and the cultural fears that shaped her final resting place. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Gene editing could replace a lifetime of medication, but there's a catch
item.description: A single gene-editing treatment could someday protect against heart disease, high cholesterol, and other common conditions for decades, potentially replacing lifelong medications. But scientists warn that permanently altering genes introduces risks that could take years to emerge, making long-term safety a critical challenge. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists trick cancer cells into making the drugs that kill them
item.description: Scientists have developed a promising new cancer-fighting strategy that uses carbon monoxide naturally produced by tumor cells to manufacture powerful drugs inside the cancer cells themselves. Early laboratory experiments suggest the technique could selectively attack cancer while sparing healthy cells, potentially paving the way for safer chemotherapy alternatives. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Who killed British archaeologist James Starkey? Archival records shed light on an 88-year-old mystery
item.description: Eighty-eight years after pioneering British archaeologist Starkey was shot dead while traveling from the ancient city of Lachish to Jerusalem, researchers say they have uncovered compelling new evidence explaining who was behind his murder—and why he was targeted. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Distinct cellular and genetic differences in colorectal cancer in young patients
item.description: Article URL: https://www.dana-farber.org/newsroom/news-releases/2026/study-reveals-distinct-cellular-and-genetic-differences-in-colorectal-cancer-in-younger-patients Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50361154 Points: 99 # Comments: 38 Fuente: Hacker News - Portada.
item.dc:creator: gmays

item.title: Researchers develop sensors for continuous corn growth monitoring
item.description: When is the best time to apply nitrogen? What plant response was there to fertilizer or any number of other treatments? There is a general answer to those questions now, but what if plant breeders and agronomists could download data from continuously monitored cornstalks and ears to develop specific answers for those questions? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: El deseo de Reid Wiseman, comandante de Artemis II, para nuevas misiones: “Estoy ansioso por ver a mis amigos continuar este legado”
item.description: Tras su regreso a la Tierra, Donald Trump le entregó a cada tripulante una medalla Medalla de Honor Espacial del Congreso, durante una ceremonia en el Centro Espacial Jonhson de Houston Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.title: A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuse’s atmosphere, new evidence suggests
item.description: Something mysterious is disturbing Betelgeuse, and astronomers believe they have identified the culprit: a hidden companion star called Siwarha. New radio observations reveal that the smaller star may be plowing through Betelgeuse’s enormous atmosphere, creating disturbances that subtly stretch and distort the red supergiant’s shape. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: One in 15 adults has experienced AI-generated image-based abuse, study finds
item.description: Around one in 15 adults has experienced AI-generated image-based abuse, according to a new study. The general-population survey of more than 7,200 adults in the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia found 7% had experienced at least one form of AI-generated image-based abuse since turning 18. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Want more social media engagement? Research suggests changing the message, not your personality
item.description: Want more engagement on social media? Stop repeating yourself. Just don't change who you are in the process. That's according to new Case Western Reserve University research suggesting that public figures can increase engagement by varying their topics and wording while "maintaining a consistent psychological voice." Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chinese scientists discover thickening ground ice in parts of warming Tibet
item.description: The Tibetan Plateau, home to the world’s largest expanse of alpine permafrost, is warming at about twice the global average but, counter-intuitively,researchers have found that ice in parts of the Tibet autonomous region is actually thickening. A team from Peking University found that shallow ground ice has unexpectedly increased over the past 20 years, affecting more than a third of the plateau’s permafrost, a phenomenon driven largely by natural climate factors. The authors noted that the... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Dannie Peng

item.title: Lab-grown neurons retain features of embryonic development
item.description: Scientists from Skoltech, together with colleagues from the Kharkevich Institute for Information Transmission Problems of the Russian Academy of Sciences, Lomonosov Moscow State University and other organizations, conducted a comparative study of the 3D genome organization in neurons derived from induced pluripotent stem cells and in neurons of the adult human brain. The authors collected and processed more than 300 3D genome maps covering 62 human samples and 34 mouse samples, including data on embryonic stem cells, induced pluripotent stem cells, neural progenitors, fetal and postmortem… Fuente: Phys.org.
